title: Compound verbs and connected speech
focus: Compound verbs (kheye nao, bole dao, chole jao), linking clauses with -e (kheye jabo), longer natural sentences.
body:
# Compound verbs and connected speech

Kolkata speech is full of **two-verb combinations**. The first verb carries the meaning and takes an **-e** ending (kheye, bole, chole, ghumiye). The second verb (nao, dao, jao, poro, phelo) changes the flavour: it adds completeness, direction or a sense of who benefits.

**The -e form** (the "conjunctive") means *having done X*: **kheye** (having eaten), **giye** (having gone), **bole** (having said), **kore** (having done), **eshe** (having come), **ghumiye** (having slept). It's the same piece you already know from **kheyechi** and **hoye geche**.

| Helper | Adds | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **nao** (take) | for yourself, go ahead | **kheye nao**: eat up |
| **dao** (give) | for someone else | **bole dao**: tell (them) for me |
| **jao** (go) | away, completely | **chole jao**: go away |
| **poro** (fall) | suddenly, into a state | **ghumiye poro**: go to sleep |
| **phelo** (throw) | finish it off | **kheye phelo**: eat it all up |

The helper takes the normal tense endings: **ghumiye poreche** (has fallen asleep), **chole geche** (has left), **bole diyechi** (I've told them).

**Linking clauses:** the -e form also joins two actions in order, like "and then": **ami kheye jabo** (I'll eat and then go), **bari giye khabo** (I'll go home and eat). Only the last verb shows the tense.

## Examples

- **kheye nao**: eat up / go ahead and eat
- **Ollie ghumiye poreche**: Ollie has fallen asleep
- **o chole geche**: he/she has left
- **ami bhule gechi**: I've forgotten
- **ami oke bole diyechi**: I've told him/her
- **amake ekta cha kore dao**: make me a cup of tea
- **Ollie sob khabar kheye pheleche**: Ollie has eaten up all the food
- **ami cha kheye boi porbo**: I'll have tea and then read a book
- **Ollie kheye ghumiye porlo**: Ollie ate and fell asleep
- **giye dekho**: go and see

## Common mistakes

- ❌ **ami khabo jabo**. Only the last verb takes the tense. The first one uses the -e form: ✅ **ami kheye jabo**.
- Mixing up **ghumiye poreche** (has fallen asleep) and **ghumocche** (is sleeping right now). Both are fine for a napping Ollie, but they mean different things.

cards.English: Eat up / go ahead and eat
cards.Notes: kheye (having eaten) + nao (take); nao = 'go ahead, for yourself'
sob = all; phelo (throw) = finish it off

cards.English: Ollie has eaten up all the food
cards.Notes: kheye + pheleche (has thrown) = has finished eating
oke = (to) him/her; bole dao = tell, on someone's behalf
bole + diyechi (I have given); oke = (to) him/her

cards.English: Make me a cup of tea
cards.Notes: amake = for me; kore dao = make (for someone); ekta sounds 'akta'
chole (having moved) + jao (go); sharp, so use with care
chole + geche (has gone) = has left for good
bhule (having forgotten) + gechi (I have gone); 'I forgot' is usually said this way
boshe (having sat) + poro (fall); more relaxed than plain bosho
ghumiye (having slept) + poro (fall) = drop off to sleep
ghumiye + poreche (has fallen); compare ghumocche = is sleeping

cards.English: Ollie has fallen asleep on the bed
cards.Notes: bichanay = on the bed; ghumiye poreche = has fallen asleep
kheye = having eaten; porlo = fell (simple past)
kheye (having eaten) + jabo (will go); also 'I'll eat before I leave'
giye (having gone) links the actions; only khabo shows the tense

cards.English: I'll have tea and then read a book
cards.Notes: cha kheye = having had tea; porbo = I'll read
giye (having gone) + dekho (see/look, to a friend)
ekbar = once; dekhe nao = have a look (for yourself)
eshe (having come) + bosho (sit, to a friend)
lit. 'having taken water, come'; niye esho = bring
